conclusion.verified_title: Input-gradient space particle inference for neural network ensembles
conclusion.title_status: Resolved from cached primary HTML title metadata only; no method-body reread.

passage_records.claim: True-label logprob gradients and normalized kernel

passages.text: We propose to use a kernel comparing the input gradients of the particles,

where \kappa is a base kernel between gradients \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x};\theta)_{y} that are of same size as the inputs \mathbf{x} . In essence, we define k as the expected similarity between the input gradients of two networks with respect to the data distribution p(\mathbf{x},y) . Interestingly, by using the kernel k , the KDE approximation \hat{\rho} of the particle distribution not only depends on the particles themselves but also depends on the data distribution. We approximate the kernel k using the training samples, with linear complexity:

The kernel only compares the gradients of the true label \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta)_{y_{n}} , as opposed to the entire Jacobian matrix \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta) , as our motivation is to encourage each particle to learn different features that could explain the training sample (\mathbf{x}_{n},y_{n}) well. This approach also reduces computational complexity, since automatic differentiation libraries such as JAX ( Bradbury et al., 2018 ) or Pytorch ( Paszke et al., 2019 ) would require \mathcal{C} passes, one per class, to calculate the full Jacobian.
We choose the RBF kernel on the unit sphere as our base kernel \kappa :

where \mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime} denote the two normalized gradients of two particles with respect to one input, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} is a diagonal matrix containing squared lengthscales. We design \kappa to be norm-agnostic since the norm of the true label gradient ||\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta)_{y_{n}}||_{2} fluctuates during training and as training converges, the log-probability f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta)_{y_{n}}=\log p(y_{n}|\mathbf{x}_{n},\theta) will approach \log 1 , leading to the norm ||\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta)_{y_{n}}||_{2} approaching 0 due to the saturation of the log-softmax activation. Furthermore, comparing the normed input gradients between ensemble members teaches them to learn complementary explanatory patterns from the training samples, which could improve robustness of the ensemble. The RBF kernel is an apt kernel to compare unit vectors ( Jayasumana et al., 2014 ) , and we can control the variances of the gradients along input dimensions via the square lengthscales \boldsymbol{\Sigma} .

passage_records.claim: Biased minibatch repulsion and extra differentiation

passages.text: To make FoRDE amenable to mini-batch gradient optimization, we adapt the kernel in Eq. 10 to a mini-batch of samples \mathcal{B}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{b},y_{b})\}_{b=1}^{B} :

In principle, this kernel in the update rule in Eq. 8 leads to biased stochastic gradients of the repulsion term because the average over batch samples in Eq. 16 is inside the logarithm. However, in practice, we found no convergence issues in our experiments.

Compared to DEs, FoRDEs take roughly three times longer to train. In addition to a forward-backward pass to calculate the log-likelihood, we need an additional forward-backward pass to calculate the input gradients, and another backward pass to calculate the gradients of the input gradient repulsion with respect to the weights. This analysis is confirmed in practice: in resnet18 / cifar-100 experiments of Section 5.2 with an ensemble size of 10, a DE took \sim 31 seconds per epoch on an Nvidia A100 GPU, while FoRDE took \sim 101 seconds per epoch.

conclusion.candidate_relationship: Normalized input gradients of true-label log probabilities and continuous particle repulsion differ from one-time graph-filtered logit-cotangent parameter VJP seeding.
conclusion.cost_limit: Paper roughly 3x DE in CIFAR100/ResNet18 K10 image experiment; no graph cost transfer.

conclusion.verified_title: HG-Adapter: Improving Pre-Trained Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks with Dual Adapters
conclusion.publication_status: arXiv v1; later venue not verified in this bounded lane
exact_read_scope: Sections2.1-2.4: typed graph definition, dual low-rank structure adapters, relation weights, label propagation and objectives; theorem statements read, proofs not audited
AppendixB algorithm; adjacent proof beginning was visible, no proof audit
AppendixD.3-D.5 downstream protocol, architecture and computing-resource claims
paper_evidence: Section2.3 Eq4 factorizes adapter W_delta=W_down W_up before ReLU; W_vartheta for same-type structure similarity is also decomposed into low-rank matrices.
Same-type homogeneous structure is a positive symmetrized k-nearest-neighbor similarity graph; adapter output A F is added to frozen post-message embeddings.
Section2.3 Eq8-10 uses another low-rank adapter and a per-target-node softmax across neighbor/relation types; its weighted neighbor representation is added to frozen heterogeneous embeddings.
Section2.4 uses training-label propagation A Y, class-subgraph contrast, feature reconstruction and a margin objective. AppendixD.3 evaluates probabilities from similarity to class-subgraph vectors.
Algorithm initializes/uploads pretraining, then tunes adapters/projection. Exact factor initialization, k, rank and initial learning-rate value are not fixed by the selected implementation paragraph.
conclusion.saved_takeaway: Low-rank graph adaptation with typed structural weighting and label-informed optimization is direct prior. It is not a BatchEnsemble committee or proof of an exact node/relation-indexed rank-one ensemble.
conclusion.candidate_relationship: Defeats novelty based on adding heterogeneity, compact adapters, task-related relation weighting or supervised graph structure alone. It adds member-specific structural propagation work if turned into an ensemble.
limitations: No author-linked implementation URL found in the retained paper HTML; exact implementation not retrieved.
The generalization theorem statements were read for method context; their proof, pseudo-label-as-extra-sample assumptions and graph-dependence conditions were not independently validated.
Published/runtime figures are source claims, not current-project resource measurements.

conclusion.verified_title: Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Pretraining for Relational Deep Learning
conclusion.publication_status: New arXiv v1 preprint; no acceptance or independent reproduction asserted
exact_read_scope: Full main method3.1-3.2 and setup4.1: temporal features, relation maps, objectives, budget and chronological evaluation
AppendixA task/database sizes and splits; B.1 validation family selection and baseline table
AppendicesC-D: full architecture/optimizer/budget/temporal encoding recipe and endpoint-adapter interaction
paper_evidence: TimeMix shares learned temporal scales/mixture weights but uses table-specific projection g_(a,k). AppendixD initializes scales at1s,1min,1h,1day and mixture logits equally.

TimeRoPE rotates source/target features in GNN messages; each relation has W_neigh^(r) and W_self^(r), then relation outputs are summed. THGFM uses relation-specific attention and a shared-space branch with endpoint adapters and type-conditioned gated fusion.

Temp-Sub uses typed mean pooling followed by type-specific learned projections and shared attention; relation-preserving edge dropout retains reverse edges jointly and at least one edge per represented relation.
Historical relation recovery uses a relation-specific bilinear decoder and removes the positive target edge and reverse from inputs; future relation activity uses cutoff-constrained horizon labels.
Five RelBench databases and11tasks use original chronological splits; four seeds42-45. HeteroGNN and THGFM were selected among five baselines using mean validation rank, not test performance.

Native recipe:3graph layers,width128; GT8heads;4-layer table ResNets; fanouts128/64/32; AdamW lr0.002 wd1e-5;100k pretraining and100k downstream steps; full encoder fine-tuning; task-metric validation checkpoint selection.
Best evaluated staged schedules depend on backbone and encodings; gains are not uniform across task types.
conclusion.saved_takeaway: A very recent heterogeneous predictive framework provides competent typed/temporal baselines and chronological evaluation. Type-specific maps, relation transforms, typed pooling, endpoint adapters and structural initialization/pretraining already coexist. It does not demonstrate a rank-one ensemble or its uncertainty benefit.
conclusion.candidate_relationship: A heterogeneous GNNM claim must earn predictive/calibration utility and charge all pretraining plus complete private graph trajectories against this recent baseline. Sharing matrices alone cannot inherit temporal/type specialization as novelty or compute savings.
limitations: Author code or dataset exports were not fetched. Exact endpoint-adapter parameterization is unspecified by the scoped passage, so rank-one equivalence with this backbone is not claimed.
Native recipe is a reference, not an admitted reproducible runtime. Text feature preparation, graph building and temporal sampling are material costs.
Data/split values are paper metadata, not verified local dataset artifacts.
